title: CLO 2024 Academic Month  CLO Virtual Garment Teaching and Research Exploration
description: Review of CLO Academic Month 2024! Ren Jinhui, a teacher from the School of Fashion Art and Engineering at Beijing Institute of Fashion Technology, prepared teaching materials based on her own software learning experience. She anticipates students' questions in advance during teaching to help them learn more effectively, and uses the virtual model editing function in CLO to simulate the body shapes of various special groups to assist design projects. Click the video to watch Teacher Ren share cases of functional clothing design assisted by CLO.
transcript:
Today, I'm going to talk about the subject of my presentation, which is the study of virtual fashion and the exploration of science and technology. As soon as you hear this, you'll understand that it consists of two parts: one is teaching, and the other is science and technology.

Today, I will share three parts. The first part is to introduce the courses related to virtual fashion, especially the one I am teaching. The second part covers the problems I encountered during my teaching process and how I solved them. The third part is about how we apply virtual fashion to science and technology. President Jia has already introduced this, so I won't go into details.

I graduated from Beijing Fashion College and then went to work at an outdoor clothing company. After that, I returned to school and gave the school’s creative products a brand name, Bift Collection. Then I went back to school again and started working on projects such as the Winter Olympics, National Day, the 70th Anniversary Exhibition, and so on. Currently, my focus is on functional clothing design, which mainly targets sportswear, clothing for disabled people, the elderly, and my classmates.

Now, I will introduce our courses. Currently, we are developing a series of courses related to virtual clothing, with several courses available. One of the courses I encountered is the digital clothing technology course. The first course was taught by Professor Ma Kai at our school, starting in 2019. Our school established the first digital experimental class in 2019.

In this experimental class, there were 30 students in the first year: 20 in design and 10 in the field of clothing factories. Their coursework was mostly the same. The 30 students in the lab took an exam in their first year, covering questions about their major, English, and some intelligence monitoring questions.

In 2019, we graduated the first digital experimental class, and last year I participated in their graduation design and thesis. Let me introduce the most closely related course we took with Kolo, called Digital Costume Textile Technology. The picture on the bottom left is one I took while teaching my students, showing a scene from class.

We have the digital experimental class, the art class, the fashion design course, and the graduate course, totaling 36 courses. During these, we teach both theory and practice, with the main emphasis on teaching the theoretical and practical aspects of these subjects. The basic principles and concepts provide knowledge of current digital and virtual costumes and some closely related concepts.

The next stage includes behavioral and physical changes of virtual models, simulation and production of common costumes, fabric textures and fabric production, scene setting and rendering, and finally, a comprehensive class assignment for homework submission.

On this page, you see some examples used during teaching. For example, in the first class, we introduce a very simple shirt or pants. We assign homework to students and then assess their level of understanding. In fact, in the previous class, we briefly introduced some applications of virtual clothing software. Most students have already been exposed to it. Additionally, some students with more interest may have learned parts of it through online teaching videos. So, we use this application to teach the students.

To understand the students' level of comprehension, it is generally not very high. Most of the students struggle. This comparison aligns with our understanding level during class. Of course, there are a few self-learning students, which is very helpful.

The bottom right corner of this page shows a virtual model and how to adjust the model’s posture in the 3D window, including changing joints and posture. The white model in the middle represents an elderly body shape. We used an OBJ file to teach students how to modify the model's body shape and apply makeup on top—this is from the virtual model perspective.

Regarding the clothing, the one in the back shows a case of revision and 2D modification before revision. The upper left one is the second example. We used Beifu’s original design cases to illustrate some points. For instance, this is from a tie pattern. We extracted the pattern from a photo and used Photoshop or PixPlant to create patterns such as magic patterns, discovery patterns, and metal patterns. We used our own case examples, including the Beifu logo.

The pink scene teaches students how to download props from other websites for scenes, how to create props themselves, and how to place characters in them. This is a demonstration of the teaching process, including some lighting and directional adjustments.

In the first eight classes, we taught about models, fabric, clothing, and so forth. At the end of the course, we assign a theme to the class for explanation. Each semester, the themes differ.

What you see now is the theme of the last semester, which ended in 2023. There were six themes: cyberpunk (a hot topic these years), cyberpunk and artificial intelligence, sustainable design, and traditional clothing restoration and innovation. These four topics have been very popular in recent years.

The festival was held at year-end because Christmas, New Year, and Spring Festival were approaching. We wanted to add themes related to the present day and rural revitalization. This rural revitalization aligns with two points: one is a project that Beifu and Di Shang Group worked on, which involved developing clothing for farmers and shepherds; the other is the theme from last year’s ACDA, a well-known design competition. We combined school projects with competition themes, which also guided our classwork. More experienced students tend to lead in these competitions.

What you see here is the class that just ended in 2023, the fashion engineering class. The science students did not design with a background in design. I noticed that students in this class tend to choose traditional clothing or themes of restoration or innovation. In contrast, students in the design class are more inclined to participate in other competitions or create innovative designs for clothing structure. These students completed their work quite seriously, with good overall composition and fashion simulation. These are traditional themes.

Some students added their own creativity. After all, they are engineering students. Although working with traditional concepts, they made some innovative designs. Here is another group, possibly a second-year group, focusing on minority ethnic clothing, where they modified patterns. There are also cyber or animation themes. The students’ understanding of cyberpunk is the fusion of machines and humans. This is related to popular games. Additionally, there are sports-themed designs.

Besides the digital clothing class, what you see now is the graduation of the 2020 class, our first digital experimental class. This student was one of my graduates last year, together with another teacher. I will show you the graduation video he made here.

You can hear the voice, right? I can hear you.

This student's design element is water. Besides the slope and wave pattern of water drops on the surface, he extracted these and made them into his folds. In the end, he used the second set of white film on the screen for the final production. This is a video of his setup.

This student was very solid in his work and is considered an excellent student among them. Besides designing water elements, his thesis connects design and research: it focuses on how to make folds in 3D software. We can see the white film picture with many folds of different types.

He combined different software—Blender, Clore, and others—to develop fold-making methods. He wrote a paper on this method. This is another student who presented last year; he was the class monitor. This student used a ceramic pattern and applied it to clothing. Initially, it became food-themed. The upper right corner shows the design that was featured in last year's fashion week, the cover of the class in Guangzhou. The middle part was made into a 3D print. This student’s thesis was about 3D printing, analyzing the process of his practice.

Now, the second part: the problems I encountered in teaching.

Firstly, different professional students have varying speeds of learning and creativity. The software has many tools, 2D and 3D windows, etc. When students first use it, they often cannot find the tools. To address this, our teaching team used many supporting tools, such as Changjiang Yu Ke Tang. These resources can only be accessed via PPT or WPI.

We record the demonstration and operation process. After class or during practice, students can watch the playback. Because some students, even after seeing the teacher’s demonstration once, still encounter problems, we record videos so they can watch repeatedly.

Secondly, based on my own experience, I summarized some methods. The problems students face are similar to those I experienced when learning the software. Being older than undergraduates, my learning speed was slower. I thought that when first using such software, it’s helpful to familiarize oneself with several tools by operating a case, writing down the process, taking screenshots of key steps, and compiling these into an instruction manual. We send this manual to students before class.

This manual also benefits students during class: some finish an operation in 10 minutes, others take an hour. Early finishers can follow the second part of the manual to explore in advance. This is more convenient. The file on the right shows screenshots of each step of my operation, which helps me prepare clear instruction manuals for students.

Thirdly, the most common problems students ask about after demonstrations include:

- Difficulty finding window tools or tools hidden in the interface;

- File transmission, such as how to import DXF and OBJ files;

- How to export rendered videos or quick photos;

- How to apply materials and textures from the drawing library to the attribute editor.

These are common initial problems.

The second type of problem is unfamiliarity with paper and craftsmanship. This class mainly consists of second- and third-year students. Sometimes the problem is not the software but lack of sewing skills or knowledge of how to assemble patterns. I myself have worked on double-layer suits or coats and faced problems like poor embroidery or backstitching, requiring reflection on my technique. This indicates a lack of solid foundational knowledge in clothing and pattern-making.

The third small issue is 3D spatial understanding. When working on multi-layer clothing or garments that twist, students often cannot distinguish front from back or left from right. For example, when moving one side to the other, they might move it from the back due to poor spatial relations. This is a common problem.

The fourth small problem is threading, cracking, and folding errors. When first learning the software, I often encountered these issues. For example, when inserting pants into a JPL file, increasing size might accidentally open seams or cause conflicts. These problems often arise.

The fifth small point is that even when emphasizing these issues in class, students still frequently make the same mistakes. Despite repeated emphasis, some students continue to encounter these problems.

The third part is how we apply virtual clothing to research.

I recently joined Beifu. One of the first projects I encountered was functional clothing for disabled people. What you see are some works from 2008 to the present. In 2008, it was called the Kangjian Clothing Research Center. Later, in 2018, it was adjusted to the Wuzhai Clothing Research Center. Now it is called the Beautiful Life Clothing Research Center.

The person you see is one of our focus subjects. Before the Beijing Winter Olympic Games, 18 to 19 years ago, I received a task from the Ministry of Science and Technology. I worked on clothing for National Team athletes for the Winter Olympics, designing garments suited to their specialized sports postures.

In the lower right corner, you can see some training clothes made for the Winter Olympic team using virtual software. There are other ongoing research projects, mainly applied to clothing for the elderly. We obtained body data and models of elderly people and used Kolo software to conduct research. This is currently in progress.

This is where teaching and science combine: some content produced by students is uploaded to the platform, building virtual models based on elderly characteristics. We also conducted experiments with white paper, which are ongoing.

The digital experimental class graduation design is based on this. Some designs were created by groups from Zhewan, still in progress. We also made pants for wheelchair users in a previous period.

That concludes my sharing today.

chunks.content: ## Introduction to Virtual Fashion Teaching and Research This section introduces the scope of virtual fashion education and its integration with science and technology, outlining the structure of the presentation focused on course introduction, teaching challenges, and research applications. Virtual fashion encompasses both teaching and scientific-technical exploration. The speaker’s presentation covers three key areas: an overview of virtual fashion-related courses, challenges encountered during instruction along with solutions, and the application of virtual fashion in scientific research. The speaker has a background from Beijing Fashion College and industry experience in outdoor clothing. They developed the "Bift Collection" brand and contributed to projects like the Winter Olympics and the 70th Anniversary Exhibition, currently focusing on functional clothing design for sportswear and special populations (disabled, elderly). --- ## Virtual Fashion Courses and Curriculum Structure This section details the curriculum development of virtual fashion courses, including the digital clothing technology course, student demographics, course content, practical assignments, and thematic class projects. Since 2019, the institution has developed a series of courses related to virtual clothing, beginning with a digital clothing technology course taught by Professor Ma Kai and the launch of the first digital experimental class with 30 students (20 design majors, 10 clothing factory majors). These students underwent exams covering their major, English, and intelligence monitoring. The curriculum spans 36 courses across experimental classes, art classes, fashion design, and graduate courses, combining theoretical and practical instruction focused on digital and virtual costume principles. Topics include: - Behavioral and physical simulation of virtual models - Fabric texture and production simulation - Scene setting and 3D rendering - Comprehensive assignments integrating learned skills Practical examples include teaching basic garments like shirts and pants, using virtual clothing software, and assessing student comprehension. Students learn to modify 3D virtual models, including posture adjustments and body shape changes using OBJ files, as well as applying makeup effects on models. Teaching integrates digital design tools such as Photoshop and PixPlant for pattern extraction and creation (magic patterns, discovery patterns, metal patterns), with original design cases such as the Beifu logo. Students also learn to download and create scene props and adjust lighting and direction in virtual environments. --- ## Thematic Class Projects and Student Work This section explains semester-based thematic projects aimed at stimulating creativity and relevance in virtual fashion design, with examples of student work reflecting diverse themes and technical skills. Each semester features different design themes; the 2023 semester included cyberpunk, cyberpunk and artificial intelligence, sustainable design, and traditional clothing restoration and innovation. Additional themes addressed contemporary topics and rural revitalization, the latter inspired by collaborations with Beifu and Di Shang Group and the ACDA design competition. Student work varies by background: engineering students tend to focus on traditional clothing with innovative modifications, while design students pursue competition-related and structurally innovative designs.

chunks.content: --- ## Thematic Class Projects and Student Work This section explains semester-based thematic projects aimed at stimulating creativity and relevance in virtual fashion design, with examples of student work reflecting diverse themes and technical skills. Each semester features different design themes; the 2023 semester included cyberpunk, cyberpunk and artificial intelligence, sustainable design, and traditional clothing restoration and innovation. Additional themes addressed contemporary topics and rural revitalization, the latter inspired by collaborations with Beifu and Di Shang Group and the ACDA design competition. Student work varies by background: engineering students tend to focus on traditional clothing with innovative modifications, while design students pursue competition-related and structurally innovative designs. Examples include: - Minority ethnic clothing pattern modifications - Cyberpunk and animation-inspired designs reflecting the fusion of humans and machines - Sports-themed clothing concepts Graduation projects from the 2020 digital experimental class highlight advanced techniques such as fold-making in 3D software and 3D printing applications. One exemplary student integrated water element motifs into garment folds using Blender and Clo3D, supported by a thesis on fold creation methods. Another student’s ceramic-patterned clothing design was featured in a major fashion week and included a 3D printed component. --- ## Teaching Challenges and Solutions in Virtual Fashion Education This section addresses common obstacles students face learning virtual fashion software and techniques, and outlines instructional strategies and resources developed to overcome these barriers. Key challenges include: 1. **Varied Learning Speeds and Software Familiarity:** Students have difficulty locating tools and navigating 2D and 3D windows. To assist, the teaching team uses supplementary resources like Changjiang Yu Ke Tang, accessible through PPT and WPI, including recorded demonstrations for repeated viewing. 2. **Instructional Manuals and Step Documentation:** The instructor compiles detailed manuals with step-by-step screenshots and operation notes, distributed before class to accommodate learners who progress at different paces. Early finishers can explore advanced content independently. 3. **Common Technical Issues:** Frequent questions concern tool location, importing DXF and OBJ files, exporting rendered videos and snapshots, and applying materials/textures via attribute editors. 4. **Knowledge Gaps in Paper and Craftsmanship:** Many students lack foundational sewing and pattern assembly skills, impacting their digital garment construction. The instructor’s own experience with multilayer garments and embroidery highlights the necessity of strong traditional craft knowledge. 5. **3D Spatial Understanding Difficulties:** Students often confuse front/back and left/right when manipulating multi-layered or twisted garments, leading to errors in positioning. 6. **Threading, Cracking, and Folding Errors:** Initial software use commonly results in seams opening or mesh conflicts, such as when adjusting sizes in JPL files. Despite repeated emphasis on these issues, some students continue to make the same mistakes, illustrating the need for ongoing reinforcement. --- ## Application of Virtual Clothing to Scientific Research This section explores the integration of virtual clothing technologies into functional apparel research, focusing on projects for disabled individuals, elderly populations, and specialized sportswear.

Despite repeated emphasis on these issues, some students continue to make the same mistakes, illustrating the need for ongoing reinforcement. --- ## Application of Virtual Clothing to Scientific Research This section explores the integration of virtual clothing technologies into functional apparel research, focusing on projects for disabled individuals, elderly populations, and specialized sportswear. The speaker joined Beifu, contributing to functional clothing research since 2008, initially at the Kangjian Clothing Research Center, later renamed the Wuzhai Clothing Research Center, and currently the Beautiful Life Clothing Research Center. Notable projects include: - Designing clothing for National Team athletes before the Beijing Winter Olympics, focusing on sports-specific posture adaptation using virtual software. - Development of training garments for Winter Olympic athletes using virtual garment simulation tools. - Ongoing research on elderly clothing, utilizing body data and 3D modeling via Kolo software to create virtual models reflecting elderly body characteristics. - Collaborative efforts between teaching and research, where student-generated virtual clothing content supports platform development and experimentation, including work with white paper prototypes. - Design projects for wheelchair users, emphasizing functional and adaptive clothing solutions. These applications demonstrate how virtual fashion education and research synergize to advance innovation in functional and adaptive garment design. --- ## Summary This document presents a comprehensive view of virtual fashion education and research as developed at Beijing Fashion College and Beifu. It covers curriculum design, practical teaching methods, student project themes, common instructional challenges, and the application of virtual clothing technology in scientific research for specialized populations. The integration of digital tools such as Blender, Clo3D, Photoshop, and Kolo software exemplifies the technical foundation supporting this evolving field.
